identity.title: Position: Probabilistic Modelling is Sufficient for Causal Inference

problem.claim: The paper addresses how causal inference questions should be answered within machine learning.

gap.claim: The authors identify confusion and prevalent claims that bespoke causal frameworks or notation are required for causal questions.

contributions.claim: Argues that any causal inference question can be addressed using probabilistic modelling and inference without causal-specific tools or notation.
Uses concrete examples to show how causal questions can be formulated by writing down the probability of everything.
Reinterprets causal tools as emerging from standard probabilistic modelling and inference, discussing their necessity and utility.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors present a general probabilistic-modelling lens as an alternative to bespoke causal frameworks and causal-specific notation.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report demonstrations through concrete examples showing causal questions tackled by explicitly specifying joint probabilities.

narrative_sequence.summary: Frames causal inference as important but surrounded by confusion about the tools required.
Identifies the widespread claim that causal-specific frameworks or notation are necessary.
Presents concrete examples based on writing down the probability of everything.
Argues that probabilistic modelling offers greater generality than bespoke causal frameworks.
Explains causal tools as outcomes of standard probabilistic modelling and inference, including their necessity and utility.

source_observation.claim: The abstract connects its central position to concrete examples formulated through explicit probability statements.

lessons.interpretation: A strong position paper can make a broad methodological claim more inspectable by tying it to explicit worked formulations.
lessons.application: For a methodological thesis, include compact examples that translate the target questions into the proposed formalism.
lessons.exception: This move may be unsuitable when examples would omit essential assumptions or when the claim depends primarily on empirical evaluation rather than formulation.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the causal questions, examples, assumptions, or comparisons used.
It does not report quantitative evaluations or detailed criteria for when causal tools are necessary or useful.
